title: Reynolds number and scale
summary: Change the speed, then change the size: which one matters for the coefficients? Five single runs of the NACA 0012 wing at 8 degrees show why wind-tunnel models work.
objectives: Compute a Reynolds number from speed, length and viscosity and say what it compares.
Show that two flows with the same Reynolds number give the same coefficients, whatever the size and speed, and that forces then scale with dynamic pressure and area.
Describe how the drag coefficient of a wing changes with Reynolds number and why WindLab's drag is high at low Reynolds numbers.

timeline.what: Objectives; prediction: what changes when the speed doubles, and when the size halves?
Three speed runs (10, 20, 40 m/s) - live or pre-computed; compute Re for each by hand.
Two size runs (chord 0.15 and 0.6 m at 20 m/s); Compare all five.
Explain: the Reynolds number, the forces in newtons, the laminar-turbulent caveat.

misconceptions: 'A smaller model gives smaller coefficients': coefficients already divide out size and speed; only the Reynolds number changes them, and only slightly.
'Doubling the speed doubles the lift': lift goes with the square of the speed; CL stays almost constant.

'Same Reynolds number means same forces': it means the same coefficients; the forces still scale with dynamic pressure times area (here the half-size wing at 20 m/s and the full-size wing at 10 m/s happen to give the same force because the factors cancel).

steps.title: What you will do
steps.text: The same wing at 8 degrees in a 10, 20 and 40 m/s wind, then a half-size and a double-size copy of it at 20 m/s. Before each run WindLab shows the Reynolds number Re = V L / nu, with L the chord and nu the viscosity of air (1.46 x 10^-5 m^2/s). You will see which of speed and size the coefficients really care about, and how the forces in newtons change.

steps.title: Predict before you run
steps.prompt: If the airspeed doubles from 20 to 40 m/s, by what factor do you expect (a) the lift force in newtons and (b) the lift coefficient to change? And if instead the wing is made half as big (chord 0.15 m, span 0.3 m) at the same 20 m/s: what happens to CL, CD and the lift force? Write your predictions.

steps.title: Explain
steps.prompt: Why do two wings of different size and speed give exactly the same coefficients when V x L is the same? And why does CD fall a little as the Reynolds number rises?
steps.text: The flow pattern around a shape depends only on the balance between the air's momentum and its viscosity, which is the Reynolds number V L / nu: same Re, same pattern, same coefficients - WindLab gives CL 0.352 and CD 0.0430 for both the half-size wing at 20 m/s and the full-size wing at 10 m/s, to every digit. The forces then follow from the coefficients: lift = CL x (1/2 rho V^2) x S, so doubling the speed quadruples the force (3.9 N, 15.9 N, 64 N) while CL hardly moves (0.352, 0.360, 0.364). The small drop of CD from 0.043 to 0.039 as Re rises is skin friction: a thinner boundary layer rubs less. One caveat: WindLab assumes the boundary layer is turbulent everywhere; a real model at these Reynolds numbers keeps laminar flow over part of the chord and has lower drag still.

steps.prompt: Doubling the airspeed from 20 to 40 m/s multiplies the lift force (in newtons) by about ...
steps.explanation: Lift = CL x (1/2 rho V^2) x S. CL changes by only about 1 %, so the force follows V^2: four times.

steps.prompt: The half-size wing at 20 m/s and the full-size wing at 10 m/s gave the same CL and CD to every digit. Why?
choices: Same Reynolds number: V x L is the same, so the flow pattern is identical
It is a coincidence of these two numbers
steps.explanation: 0.15 m x 20 m/s = 0.3 m x 10 m/s. With the same Reynolds number the two flows are scaled copies of each other, so every coefficient agrees. This is the principle behind wind-tunnel models.

steps.prompt: From Re 2 x 10^5 to 8 x 10^5 the drag coefficient fell from 0.043 to 0.039 while CL barely changed. The best explanation is ...
choices: Skin friction falls as the Reynolds number rises, and it is a good share of the drag
Lift and drag always fall together
The mesh was coarser at high speed
steps.explanation: The friction coefficient of a turbulent boundary layer falls slowly with Reynolds number (roughly as Re to the power -1/5). Pressure and induced drag hardly change.

steps.title: Homework (optional)
steps.text: Run the full-size wing at 5 m/s and at 80 m/s (Re about 1 x 10^5 and 1.6 x 10^6) and add them to the comparison. Does the trend in CD continue? Then read the 'Why this range?' note next to CD: at low Reynolds numbers a real wing has a laminar boundary layer over part of the chord, so measured drag is 20-40 % lower than WindLab's fully turbulent result.
